# Pi ↔ MCU protocol (Generated by Claude)

The protocol between the Raspberry Pi (Python) and the STM32 Nucleo-G431RB
(C++), written step by step. Steps 1–3 are done: the CRC, the receive and
transmit buffers, and sealed lines.

```
Pi (Python)                                   MCU (C++)
seal(body)  ──── UART ────►  RX interrupt -> RingBuffer -> LineReader -> unseal -> body
unseal(line) ◄─── UART ────  DMA <- RingBuffer (TX) <- seal(buf, len) <- body
```

## Language and tools

| What                      | Version                                          |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| C++ standard              | **C++23** (`-std=c++23`)                         |
| PC compiler               | `g++-14` (GCC 14.3)                              |
| MCU compiler              | `arm-none-eabi-g++` 14.3.1 (GNU Tools for STM32, in STM32CubeIDE) |
| Python                    | 3.10 or newer (uses `str \| None`)               |

Why C++23 and GCC 14:

- `std::span` (C++20) and `std::string_view` pass a pointer and a length as one
  object, with no copy.
- `std::string_view::contains` (C++23) is used in `unseal`.
- `<print>` (`std::println`) is used by the PC tests and needs GCC 14. It stays
  out of the firmware because it adds tens of KB of flash.

Rules for code that runs on the MCU:

- no heap: no `new`, `std::vector`, `std::string`
- no exceptions, no RTTI: build with `-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti`
- every function is `noexcept`; sizes are template parameters or `constexpr`
- no `<iostream>` or `<print>`

Recommended flags for PC test builds:

```
g++-14 -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion -Werror=return-type -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
```

`-Werror=return-type` turns a missing `return` into an error.
`-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` makes `std::array`, `std::span` and `std::string_view`
check every `[]` index. It is a debugging flag only, so don't use it on the MCU.

## Wire format

Every message is one line of ASCII text, the same in both directions:

```
<body>*XXXX\r\n
 │      │   └─ end of line: '\n' ends it, '\r' is optional on receive
 │      └──── crc16(body) as 4 uppercase hex digits
 └─────────── ASCII text; may contain '*', never '\r' or '\n'
```

Example: `2 0 5 hello*EBDC\r\n`.

Python and C++ accept exactly the same lines. This was checked on 4609 lines,
including every possible single-byte change of a sealed line.

## 1. CRC-16

Every line carries a CRC, so the receiver can tell a line damaged on the UART
(a flipped bit, a lost byte) from a good one, and drop it instead of acting on
it.

### Parameters

| Parameter     | Value                         |
|---------------|-------------------------------|
| Name          | CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE            |
| Width         | 16 bits                       |
| Polynomial    | `0x1021` (x¹⁶ + x¹² + x⁵ + 1) |
| Initial value | `0xFFFF`                      |
| Bit order     | MSB first, no reflection      |
| Final XOR     | none                          |
| Check value   | `"123456789"` → `0x29B1`      |

Any implementation with these parameters matches ours. In Python, the built-in
one is `binascii.crc_hqx(data, 0xFFFF)`.

### Algorithm

1. Start with `crc = 0xFFFF`.
2. For each byte, XOR it into the top 8 bits of `crc`.
3. Repeat 8 times: remember the top bit, shift `crc` left by 1, and if the top
   bit was 1, XOR in `0x1021`. Keep `crc` 16 bits wide.
4. After the last byte, `crc` is the result.

### C++ interface (`crc16.hpp`)

```cpp
constexpr std::uint16_t crc16_update(std::uint16_t crc, std::uint8_t byte) noexcept;  // one byte
constexpr std::uint16_t crc16(std::span<const std::uint8_t> data) noexcept;          // raw bytes
constexpr std::uint16_t crc16(std::string_view text) noexcept;                       // text
constexpr std::array<char, 4> crc_to_hex(std::uint16_t crc) noexcept;                // 0xEBDC -> "EBDC"
```

Everything is `constexpr`, so `static_assert(crc16("123456789") == 0x29B1)` is
checked while compiling. The text overload casts each `char` with
`static_cast<std::uint8_t>`, because `reinterpret_cast` is not allowed at
compile time.

### What it detects

- every 1-bit and 2-bit error
- every odd number of flipped bits
- every burst of errors up to 16 bits long

It is not security: anyone can compute a matching CRC for a changed line.

### Test values

| Input           | CRC    |
|-----------------|--------|
| `""` (empty)    | `FFFF` |
| `"A"`           | `B915` |
| `"123456789"`   | `29B1` |
| `"0"`           | `D7A3` |
| `"2 0 5 hello"` | `EBDC` |

## 2. RingBuffer (`ring_buffer.hpp`)

`RingBuffer<M>` is a byte queue with **one writer and one reader** and no lock.
It is used twice on the MCU:

| Ring | Writer (owns `REAR`)              | Reader (owns `FRONT`)                       |
|------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| RX   | UART receive interrupt: `push(byte)` | main loop: `pop(byte)`, `clear_buffer()` |
| TX   | main loop: `push(span)`           | the DMA side: `waiting()` + `free_bytes(n)` |

```cpp
template <std::size_t M>            // M slots, a power of two; holds up to M bytes
class RingBuffer {
    bool push(std::uint8_t byte) noexcept;                        // writer
    bool push(std::span<const std::uint8_t> data) noexcept;       // writer: all or nothing
    bool pop(std::uint8_t& byte) noexcept;                        // reader
    std::span<const std::uint8_t> waiting() const noexcept;       // reader: next contiguous block
    [[nodiscard]] bool free_bytes(std::size_t n) noexcept;        // reader: n bytes done
    void clear_buffer() noexcept;                                 // reader: FRONT = REAR
    std::size_t size() const noexcept;                            // bytes waiting (a snapshot)
    std::size_t dropped() const noexcept;                         // bytes refused because full
};
```

How it works:

- **The indices are free-running.** They only count up, and the array is
  indexed with `i & (M - 1)`. `REAR - FRONT` is the number of bytes waiting, so
  all M cells are usable, and unsigned wrap-around keeps it correct. This is why
  M must be a power of two.
- **Each index has exactly one writer.** Each side reads its own index
  `relaxed`, reads the other side's index with `acquire`, touches the data, and
  then publishes its own index with `release`. The data is therefore always
  written before the index that makes it visible.
- **`waiting()` + `free_bytes()` is a pop without a copy.** The DMA sends
  straight from the buffer, and the space is freed only after it has been sent.
  If the data wraps around the end, `waiting()` returns the part up to the end
  first.
- **Compile-time checks:** `M >= 1`, M is a power of two, and
  `std::atomic<std::size_t>` is lock-free. A lock inside an interrupt could
  deadlock.

Cost on the Cortex-M4 (`-O2`): `RingBuffer<512>` with `push`/`pop` takes 108 B
of flash and 524 B of RAM.

## 3. Sealed lines

### Python (`line.py`)

```python
seal(body: str) -> bytes            # b"<body>*XXXX\r\n"; ValueError for \r, \n or non-ASCII
unseal(line: bytes) -> str | None   # the body, or None if the line is damaged
```

### C++ (`seal.hpp`)

```cpp
inline constexpr std::size_t CRC_SIZE      = 4;                  // XXXX
inline constexpr std::size_t STAR_CRC_SIZE = CRC_SIZE + 1;       // *XXXX
inline constexpr std::size_t SEAL_SIZE     = STAR_CRC_SIZE + 2;  // *XXXX\r\n

// The body is already at the start of buf; append "*XXXX\r\n" after it, in place.
// Returns the whole line, or an empty view if the body is invalid or buf is too small.
[[nodiscard]] constexpr std::string_view seal(std::span<char> buf, std::size_t len) noexcept;

// The body of a sealed line, or std::nullopt if the line is damaged.
// The body points into line's buffer: it is valid only while that buffer is unchanged.
[[nodiscard]] constexpr std::optional<std::string_view> unseal(std::string_view line) noexcept;
```

- **`seal` works in place:** the caller builds the body in the transmit buffer,
  and `seal` only adds 7 bytes. Nothing is copied.
- **`unseal` returns a view:** the body is not copied either.

`unseal` rejects a line when any of these holds:

1. after removing `\n` and then `\r`, it is shorter than 5 bytes, or the
   character 5 from the end is not `*`;
2. the body contains `\r` or `\n`;
3. the 4 characters after `*` are not exactly `crc_to_hex(crc16(body))`
   (uppercase only);
4. the body contains a byte above 127.

### LineReader (`line_reader.hpp`)

It turns the stream of received bytes into complete lines. It sits between the
RX `RingBuffer` and `unseal`:

```cpp
template <std::size_t N>            // the longest line accepted, without "\r\n"
class LineReader {
    bool feed(std::uint8_t byte) noexcept;          // true exactly when this byte completed a line
    std::string_view line() const noexcept;         // that line; valid until the next feed()
    std::size_t dropped() const noexcept;           // lines dropped for being longer than N
    static constexpr std::size_t capacity() noexcept;  // N
};
```

- **This is where bytes become text:** `static_cast<char>(byte)`.
- **Line endings:** `\n` ends a line, `\r` is skipped, and empty lines are
  ignored.
- **Too-long lines:** a line longer than N is dropped, and everything up to the
  next `\n` is ignored, so the reader resynchronises exactly at the next real
  line.

The main loop on the MCU:

```cpp
std::uint8_t byte;
while (rx.pop(byte)) {
    if (reader.feed(byte)) {
        if (auto body = unseal(reader.line())) handle(*body);
        else ++bad_lines;
    }
}
```

## Running the tests

```
python3 test_crc16.py; echo $?

g++-14 -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion test_crc16.cpp -o test_crc16_cpp && ./test_crc16_cpp; echo $?
```

Each one exits with 0 when every test passes.

| Test             | What it checks                                                       |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `test_crc16.py`  | the 5 values above, plus 1000 random inputs compared with `binascii` |
| `test_crc16.cpp` | the 5 values with `static_assert` (while compiling) and at run time   |

Sanitizers catch bugs that a passing test can hide. Use them for PC test builds
only, never on the MCU:

- `-fsanitize=address,undefined` finds out-of-bounds accesses, use of freed or
  out-of-scope memory, and undefined behaviour such as signed overflow.
- `-fsanitize=thread` finds data races. Use it for any test that runs a writer
  and a reader on two threads (the `RingBuffer` case). It can't be combined
  with `address`, so build it separately.
